1
AUTHORIZES BONDS FOR HOUSING AFFORDABILITY PROGRAMS. LEGISLATIVE STATUTE.
ARGUMENT IN FAVOR OF PROPOSITION 1
YES ON PROP. 1: AFFORDABLE HOMES FOR VETERANS, SENIORS, PEOPLE WITH DISABILITIES AND WORKING FAMILIES-WITHOUT RAISING TAXES
All Californians deserve a safe and affordable place to call home, but California has a housing shortage that is driving the nation’s worst housing affordability crisis. More than half of renters spend over 30% of their income on rent and only 22% of households can afford a median-priced home, yet only 1% of California’s state budget goes to housing.
Prop. 1 gives Californians the opportunity to:
Fast-track housing production;
Provide housing to working families, veterans, people with disabilities and seniors;
Help prevent homelessness by keeping our most vulnerable neighbors in their homes;
Expands homeownership opportunities;
Maintains strict fiscal accountability and transparency with NO NEW TAXES.
PROP. 1 HONORS OUR VETERANS
Dedicates $1.25 billion solely to veterans’ housing and homeownership opportunities through the existing CalVet Home Loan Program, which has already helped almost a million veterans and their families.
“California has one of the largest populations of homeless veterans in the nation. After their service, our veterans deserve a place to call home. Prop. 1 delivers on that promise.”-Michael Blecker, President, CA Association of Veteran Service Agencies
PROP. 1 BUILDS HOMES LOW- AND MIDDLE-INCOME FAMILIES CAN AFFORD
Prop. 1 jumpstarts the construction of tens of thousands of shovel-ready affordable homes across California, quickly turning stalled construction into move-in ready homes. The teacher in your child’s classroom, the firefighter who protects your neighborhood, first-time homebuyers, low- and middle-income Californians, and the nurse at your local hospital can no longer afford to live in most California communities. Prop. 1 builds more homes working people can actually afford.
NO NEW TAXES-STRICT ACCOUNTABILITY AND TRANSPARENCY
Prop. 1 doesn’t raise taxes and every dollar comes with strict accountability and public reporting. Voters will be able to see exactly how many homes get built, where, and at what cost. Prop. 1 unlocks federal matching funds, bringing tax dollars we send to Washington back home to California.
PROP. 1 HELPS SENIORS, VETERANS & OUR MOST VULNERABLE
Prop. 1 creates and preserves housing to help those who are one crisis away from homelessness stay off the streets, low-income seniors on fixed incomes, survivors of domestic violence and their families, veterans, at risk and foster youth, and people with disabilities who all deserve safe and stable homes.
PROP. 1 INVESTS IN COMMUNITIES & ESSENTIAL WORKERS
Quality, affordable housing is the foundation of thriving communities. Prop. 1 strengthens that foundation by helping essential workers-from firefighters and teachers to nurses-afford to live in the communities they serve. Working families and essential workers across California are being priced out and left behind. Prop. 1 enables the construction of affordable housing for these essential workers who dedicate their lives to our communities.
YES ON PROP. 1: SUPPORTED BY VETERANS, SENIORS, TEACHERS, FIREFIGHTERS, AND AFFORDABLE HOUSING ADVOCATES including Habitat for Humanity California, California Alliance for Retired Americans, Housing California, California Housing Consortium, California Alliance of Child and Family Services.
VOTE YES ON PROP. 1, Veterans and Affordable Housing Bond, to honor those veterans who served; provide safe and stable housing to California’s most vulnerable; guarantee strict fiscal accountability with no new taxes; and build the affordable homes all Californians deserve.

Photo by Damian Dovarganes, AP Photo In summary Supporters say California desperately needs money to fund housing construction and make a dent in its homelessness and affordability crisis. Critics say bond financing isn’t the way to do it. Follow the election results in California: Sign up for our newsletter (https://calmatters.org/subscribe-to-calmatters/california-election-newsletter/) to receive alerts when the contests for governor, Prop. 40, insurance commissioner and other key results are called. For years, California has grappled with a problem that has affected nearly every aspect of our society: The state doesn’t have enough homes that people can afford to live in. Proposition 1 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-1-housing-bond/) aims to address that crisis. It’s estimated that more than 180,000 Californians (https://calmatters.org/housing/homelessness/2026/05/point-in-time-homelessness-report/) are homeless. Rents are so high that a minimum wage worker would need to work 102 hours a week (https://nlihc.org/oor/state/ca) to afford a typical one-bedroom apartment, according to the National Low Income Housing Coalition. A big piece of that problem is construction: Not enough homes are being built. Fewer than a third (https://calmatters.org/housing/2026/08/california-rhna-housing-affordable-progress/) of California cities and counties are on track to permit enough market-rate housing to hit their state-mandated targets, and fewer than 6% are on track for very low-income housing. Those targets are based on the state’s assumption that we need nearly 2.5 million more homes. Legislators have passed multiple laws (https://calmatters.org/housing/2025/10/newsom-signs-massive-california-housing-overhaul/) trying to address that (https://calmatters.org/education/2026/10/new-laws-affordable-student-housing-california/) by making it easier, faster and cheaper to get projects permitted (https://calmatters.org/housing/2025/06/ceqa-urban-development-infill-budget/) and built. Prop. 1 is supposed to supply the money. A recent report estimated (https://calmatters.org/housing/2026/03/affordable-housing-bottleneck/) nearly 40,000 affordable units throughout California have been designed, permitted and partially funded and are sitting stalled because developers just can’t quite get enough money to build them. What would Prop. 1 do? If it passes, Prop. 1 would allow the state to sell $11.25 billion in general obligation bonds to fund various types of housing, including homes for veterans, homeless Californians, renters, homeowners, farmworkers, students and tribes. Where would the money go? Prop. 1 would fund a variety of programs. Here’s how it breaks down: $7.2 billion to buy, build or renovate apartment buildings, generally through low-interest loans to developers. Projects funded this way would have to reserve a certain number of units for low-income households. Some would be used for “supportive housing,” homeless housing that includes additional services. This, in combination with other funding sources, would help support up to 40,000 rental units, according to (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop1-110326.pdf) the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office. $1.25 billion to help veterans secure loans to buy homes. $1.1 billion to help low and moderate-income households buy homes. $500 million for the infrastructure that supports new housing construction, such as water, sewage, parks and transportation improvements. $450 million to build or renovate an estimated 2,500 units of farmworker housing. $350 million to fund affordable homes for an estimated 1,200 University of California and California State University students. $200 million in housing grants to tribes, which could fund both home construction and renovation. $200 million up for grabs to cities, counties and other groups that pitch pilot projects to develop low-cost housing. How would California pay for it? It would cost the state between $500 million and $600 million each year for about 25 years to repay the cost of the general housing bond, according to the legislative analyst. That money would come from the state’s general fund, and factors in interest. The $1.25 billion for veterans housing would not cost the state anything, as participating vets would pay it off through monthly loan payments. Have we done anything like this before? California voters approved (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2024/03/election-result-proposition-1/) (by the slimmest of margins) another bond (https://calmatters.org/housing/homelessness/2026/03/prop-1-update/) in 2024 that provided $2 billion to fund homes (https://calmatters.org/health/mental-health/2025/06/prop-1-mental-health-awards/) for people who need mental health and addiction services and veterans. That 2024 bond also was dubbed Prop. 1. What do supporters say? Supporters include housing developers and advocates, veterans groups, the California State University and University of California boards, groups representing California’s cities and counties, Democratic legislators and Gov. Gavin Newsom. Donors backing Prop. 1 also reflect some who would benefit. The campaign has received more than $12 million, including about $2 million from carpenters’ unions, $1 million from Airbnb and $1 million from Building a Better California, a PAC funded by Google founder Sergey Brin and other Silicon Valley billionaires. Sign up for free Δ Vivian Wan, chief executive of affordable housing provider Abode, says her organization has four projects with a planned total of about 230 units in the works that she hopes Prop. 1 will fund. Three are in the Bay Area and one is in Yolo County. Without that cash infusion, all four projects are stalled, she said. Projects for homeless and low-income residents need large subsidies since their tenants don’t pay enough in rent to offset the cost of building. They often also have to fund additional services, such as case managers to help residents navigate their physical and mental health, addictions, finances and more. City and county dollars can pay for some but not all of that. Prop. 1 would be “huge,” Wan said. But it wouldn’t magically solve the housing crisis. “Is it enough? Absolutely not,” she said. “We are lightyears behind in terms of production to meet the need. We have underinvested in housing for decades. This is going to help, for sure, but we really need a permanent source.” What do opponents say? When this measure (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/bills/ca_202520260sb417) came up for a floor vote before the Legislature, two Republican senators voted no, as well as seven Republican assemblymembers. Sen. Tony Strickland (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/legislators/tony-strickland-188489), a Republican from Huntington Beach who opposed the bill, said calling it “The Veterans and Affordable Housing Bond Act of 2026” amounted to a bait-and-switch maneuver, as only a small fraction of the total funds go to vets. “It really just says that you’re using veterans to pass your $10 billion general obligation bond,” he said during a June hearing. And, he said, there are better ways to get families into housing than using a bond to “borrow money against the future.” The strong revenues California experienced this year won’t continue, making it risky to push the state deeper into debt, he said. Statute.
ANALYSIS OF MEASURE
BACKGROUND
Public Sector Funds Some Home Building. In most years, about 100,000 houses and
apartments are built in California. Most of these housing units are built entirely with private
dollars. Some, however, receive financial help from federal, state, or local governments. In the
case of housing funded by the state, the state government generally provides local governments,
nonprofit organizations, and private developers with grants or low-cost loans to fund a portion of
the housing units’ construction costs. Typically, housing built with these funds must be sold or
rented to Californians with low incomes.
Bonds Are a Common Way for the State to Fund Home Building and Homeownership
Programs. Over the past few decades, the state has used general obligation bonds to fund various
housing programs. Bonds are a way the state borrows money to cover the up-front costs of a
development and then repays the money plus interest over time. The last statewide general
obligation bond for affordable housing was approved by voters in 2024, providing $2 billion to
provide housing for veterans and other people with mental health or substance use challenges
who are facing homelessness.
Home Loan Program for Veterans. The state’s veterans home loan program provides home
loans to eligible veterans, including veterans who may not otherwise qualify for a home loan.
Under the program, the state sells general obligation bonds to investors and uses the funds to
provide loans to veterans to purchase homes. Participating veterans repay the cost of the bonds
through their payments on their home loan. The last statewide general obligation bond for
veterans home loans was approved by voters in 2018, which provided $1 billion for the program.

$11.25 billion in general obligation bonds for housing purposes. This amount consists of (1) a
$10 billion bond for a variety of state housing programs that would be repaid by the General
Fund and (2) a $1.25 billion bond that would be repaid by veterans’ payments on their home
loans. (The General Fund is the account the state uses to pay for most public services, including
education, health care, and prisons. For more information on the state’s General Fund-supported
bonds, please see “Overview of State Bond Debt” later in this guide.)

programs, which are summarized in Figure 1. The funds would be allocated over a number of

• Affordable Multifamily Housing Programs. Proposition 1 provides $7.2 billion to
acquire, build, or renovate rental housing, such as apartment buildings. These
programs generally provide local governments and private developers with low-
interest loans to fund part of the project cost. In exchange, projects generally must
reserve units for low-income households for a period of 55 years. Some of this
funding would be used for supportive housing, which provides on-site services (such
as mental health and substance use counseling) to certain residents.
• Homeownership Programs. Proposition 1 provides $1.1 billion to support
homeownership for low- and moderate-income households. Some of the funds would
be used to provide homebuying assistance for first-time homebuyers through loans
that generally do not have to be paid back until the home is sold or paid off. Other
funds would be provided to nonprofit organizations and other entities for activities
such as acquiring land to build homes for eligible low-income homebuyers and
repairing existing homes owned by low-income households.
• Infrastructure Programs. Proposition 1 provides $500 million for a variety of
infrastructure projects to support affordable housing developments, such as water,
sewage, parks, and transportation improvements.
• Farmworker Housing Program. Proposition 1 provides $450 million in loans and
grants to build or renovate housing for farmworkers. Program funds could be used for
both rental and owner-occupied housing.
• Higher Education Student Housing Programs. Proposition 1 provides $350 million,
split evenly between the University of California and California State University, for
affordable student housing.
• Tribal Housing Program. Proposition 1 provides $200 million in grants to tribes.
Funds could be used for various housing-related purposes, including construction and
repair of rental and owner-occupied housing.
• Local Pilot Programs. Proposition 1 provides $200 million that would be available to
cities, counties, and certain other entities for pilot projects aimed at developing
housing at reduced costs.
November 3, 2026 Ballot
Page 3 of 4
Veterans Housing Program. Proposition 1 also provides $1.25 billion for home loan
assistance to veterans. Veterans generally use these loans to purchase single-family residences,
condominiums, farms, and mobile homes.
FISCAL EFFECTS
Increased State Cost to Repay the $10 Billion Bond for Housing Programs. The state
General Fund cost to repay the bond would be $500 million to $600 million annually for about
25 years. The estimated annual cost would be about one-quarter of 1 percent (0.25 percent) of
the state’s total General Fund budget. Since the state has to pay interest on the money it borrows,
the total cost of the bond would be about 15 percent more (after adjusting for inflation) than if
the state paid up front with money it already has.
No Direct State Cost for Veterans Housing Program. Veterans participating in the home
loan program would make monthly payments to the state, allowing the state to repay the bonds.
These payments have always covered the amount owed on the bonds, meaning the program has
always operated at no direct cost to the state.
Administrative Costs. A number of state entities would experience increased costs to
administer the various housing programs. A portion of the bond funds would cover these costs.
Impact of Funds. Much of the funding from Proposition 1 would be used together with other
government monies to provide housing assistance. The bond funds would provide subsidies for
up to 40,000 multifamily rental units, as well as about 2,500 units for farmworkers and about
1,200 beds for university students. The funds also would help up to 40,000 households, including
about 2,100 veterans, with homeownership by providing homebuyer assistance and supporting
the production and repair of homes.
November 3, 2026 Ballot
Page 4 of 4
YES/NO STATEMENT
A YES vote on this measure means: The state could borrow $11.25 billion to support
veterans and affordable housing.
A NO vote on this measure means: The state could not borrow $11.25 billion to support
veterans and affordable housing.
SUMMARY OF LEGISLATIVE ANALYST’S ESTIMATE OF NET STATE AND
LOCAL GOVERNMENT FISCAL IMPACT
• Increased state cost of $500 million to $600 million annually for about 25 years to repay
the housing bond.
BALLOT LABEL
Fiscal Impact: Increased state cost of $500 million to $600 million annually for about 25
years to repay the housing bond.

Proposition 1: Housing Affordability
Proposition 1: Housing Affordability
Proposition 1: Authorizes Bonds For Housing Affordability Programs. Legislative Statute.
Additional Titles
Cali fornia Proposition 1, Veteran and Housing Assistance Programs Bond Measure
Summary
Proposition 1 is a legislatively referred bond measure which was passed by the California Legislature on June 26, 2026, through Senate Bill 417 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260SB417) (SB 417). Both the Assembly and Senate votes exceeded the two-thirds majority required for the Legislature to place a bond measure before voters. Because legislatively referred bond measures also require the governor’s approval, Gov. Gavin Newsom’s signature on SB 417 completed the process of placing Proposition 1 on the ballot.
Proposition 1 would allow California to sell $11.25 billion through state bonds for housing programs. Of that amount, $10 billion would go toward housing assistance for low- and moderate-income Californians that would be repaid by the General Fund, while $1.25 billion would support the state’s home loan program for veterans.
The $10 billion for housing would fund a range of projects, including affordable rental housing, assistance for first-time homebuyers, farmworker and student housing, housing infrastructure, tribal housing projects, and local pilot programs aimed at lowering housing costs.
F iscal Impact
(Summary of Legislative Analyst's Estimate of Net State and Local Government Fiscal Impact)
The state would repay the $10 billion housing portion from the General Fund, at an estimated cost of $500 million to $600 million a year for about 25 years. Veterans participating in the loan program would repay their home loans to the state. These payments are then used to pay back the bonds.
Because the state has to pay interest when it borrows money, the bond would cost about 15 percent more, after adjusting for inflation, than paying for the projects up front with money the state already has.
What your vote means (LAO's Analysis)
A YES vote on this measure means: The state could issue $11.25 billion in bonds to support housing programs for income-qualified Californians.
A NO vote on this measure means: The state would not issue the proposed $11.25 billion in bonds for low-income housing programs.

Pro/Con Statements
Pro Con
Proponents argue that California’s housing affordability and homelessness crises require substantial public investment and that Proposition 1 would directly improve the lives of people struggling to find or keep stable housing. They contend that funding affordable housing construction and preservation, homeownership assistance, and housing for veterans, farmworkers, students, and homeless and foster youth would provide meaningful help to Californians most affected by high housing costs.
Opponents argue that California should not take on additional debt for housing when the state has substantial revenues and could fund these programs directly. They contend that the underlying housing problem is a shortage of available homes caused largely by regulations and development restrictions, rather than a lack of government spending on affordable housing.

Key fiscal context: California's debt-service ratio is ~3% of General Fund revenues, below the historical average of ~4%. Adding Prop 1 ($500-600M/yr) and Prop 38 ($500-600M/yr) would bring it to roughly 3.5% — still within historical norms. Treasurer's Debt Affordability Report Oct 2026 says 3.41% in 2025-26, estimated 3.83% in 2026-27 (that's using gross debt service without offsets; with offsets ~2.8%).

Also important: leverage. Enterprise report: every $1 of state funds leverages ~$3.60 of local/federal/private funds. Clearing the backlog requires $4.1B extra. Prop 1 provides $10B — more than enough to clear the current backlog and continue.

Cost per unit: $7.2B for up to 40,000 units = $180,000/unit in state subsidy, which leverages total development costs. That's decent value.

Now let me check the California Budget & Policy Center brief and also see whether there's any concern about the bond money being diverted/admin costs, plus accountability provisions. Also let me check LA Times editorial board position (they may have endorsed Yes).

Let me also weigh: The con argument from SD Union-Tribune: "subsidized shelter can't solve the housing crisis" — a Terner Center / market-urbanist view. But note the counter: Prop 45 (CEQA streamlining) is also on the ballot. Also, importantly, the state has already passed streamlining laws.

Another key consideration: opportunity cost given the structural deficit ($18B in 2026-27, growing to $35B by 2027-28 per LAO). $500-600M is 0.25% of the General Fund — small relative to the deficit, but it is a fixed obligation.

Also, the measure doesn't raise taxes and debt service is small. California historically uses bonds for capital investments, and affordable housing is a long-lived capital asset (55-year affordability covenant), so borrowing against a 55-year asset with 25-30 year repayment is actually fiscally appropriate (intergenerational equity argument).

Proposition 1: California’s Veterans and Affordable Housing Bond
A $11.25 Billion Bond to Continue Building Affordable Homes for Californians
July 2026 | By Monica Davalos (https://calbudgetcenter.org/people/monica-davalos/)
Print Report
key takeaway
Proposition 1, appearing on the November 2026 ballot, would provide funding for affordable housing and accessible homeownership. Prop. 1 asks voters to authorize a $11.25 billion general obligation bond to fund programs that support the creation and preservation of affordable housing, expand homebuying opportunities for low- and moderate-income Californians and veterans, and invest in permanent solutions to solve homelessness. If Prop. 1 is approved, it would replenish funding for several successful state programs that have exhausted their resources. Prop. 1 was placed on the ballot by the Legislature through passage of Senate Bill 417 (2026) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260SB417).

Over the past six years, California has nearly tripled (https://calhousingpartnership.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/03/CHP_2026-Housing-Needs-Report-FINAL.pdf) the number of new affordable homes it funds. Yet the state continues to face a severe shortage of affordable housing, particularly for Californians with the lowest incomes. California needs more than 2.5 million new homes, including at least 1 million homes that are affordable to lower-income households. Housing cost pressures fall hardest on California renters as nearly half pay unaffordable rents — a hardship that disproportionately impacts Black and Latinx renters with low incomes, older adults, mixed-status families, and people with disabilities.
Unlike market-rate or luxury housing, affordable housing projects typically cannot be built without subsidies because affordable rents do not generate enough revenue to cover development or operating costs. As a result, affordable housing projects rely on multiple funding streams to close financing gaps. Currently, more than 46,000 affordable homes across California (491 developments) (https://www.enterprisecommunity.org/sites/default/files/2024-04/State_Pipeline_2024_FINAL.pdf) are waiting for the last bit of state funding needed to break ground. Prop. 1 would provide funding for various programs that help bridge the financial gap to keep affordable housing construction moving.
Why Is Affordable Housing Funding Running Out & How Would Prop. 1 Help?
Despite the ongoing housing affordability challenges Californians are facing, state funding for affordable housing has largely disappeared. Over the past several years, affordable housing programs have relied on one-time General Fund investments (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/protecting-progress-state-housing-and-homelessness-funding-must-continue/) to supplement voter-approved housing bonds, but those investments have drastically declined. The 2026 Budget Act only includes one-time investments in two significant affordable housing programs: $500 million for state Low Income Housing Tax Credits and $200 million for the Multifamily Housing Program, effectively leaving multiple programs (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/first-look-understanding-the-governors-proposed-2026-27-california-budget/#h-proposed-budget-includes-no-new-state-funding-for-affordable-housing) without additional funds. Beyond these investments, there is no meaningful ongoing or one-time investment from the state General Fund for affordable housing development.
The state’s remaining modest affordable housing funding sources, including the Affordable Housing and Sustainable Communities Program (AHSC), funded through Cap-and-Invest; state and federal Low-Income Housing Tax Credits; and SB 2 planning funds are insufficient to meet the demand and often require additional funding to be fully leveraged. The AHSC program was expected to receive nearly $800 million per year for affordable housing, but recent changes by the California Air Resources Board put that funding at risk.
Curious About Other Ballot Propositions?
Browse our collection of resources covering California’s statewide ballot measures to help you understand what’s at stake for California this November.
See More Resources (https://calbudgetcenter.org/issues/ballot-propositions/)
The funding approved by voters through the 2018 Veterans and Affordable Housing Bond Act has been fully committed — exhausted within five years, by the end of 2023, due to overwhelming demand. The state’s flagship Multifamily Housing Program, which relied on funding from the bond and one-time General Fund investments, is routinely oversubscribed by roughly 9 to 1. Together these signal that the barrier to building more affordable housing in California isn’t a lack of will or projects — it’s a lack of sustainable funding.
Without new state investments, affordable housing production will stall just as California is making meaningful progress and as federal cuts threaten to make it even more difficult for Californians to make ends meet, which is why state lawmakers placed Prop. 1 on the ballot.
What Affordable Housing and Homeownership Programs Would Prop. 1 Fund?
Prop. 1 asks voters to authorize $11.25 billion in general obligation (GO) bonds that would support the construction and preservation of affordable rental homes, expand homeownership assistance for low- and moderate-income homebuyers, including veterans, and provide permanent housing for people at risk of or experiencing homelessness. Within these categories, it would provide some funding for programs that serve distinct populations, such as California tribes, farmworkers, unhoused youth, and college students. The bond funds would be allocated as follows:
Affordable Housing Development and Preservation
$5.1 billion for the Multifamily Housing Program (MHP) , which supports the construction, rehabilitation, or preservation of affordable rental housing. At least 10% of units in a MHP development must be available for extremely low-income households who are at the highest risk of facing homelessness. This is one of California’s model affordable housing development programs.
$1.15 billion for supportive housing through the MHP program. Supportive housing provides stable homes with wrap-around services for people who were chronically homeless or at risk of becoming so. These funds can be used for operating subsidy reserves, which are critical to the longevity and sustainability of permanent supportive housing.
Up to 15% — $150 million — would be allocated as grants to acquire or build permanent supportive housing among other specified uses.
Another $150 million is carved out for the capital development or acquisition of youth housing through MHP. This would serve current or former foster youth, homeless minors or youth, or youth at risk of homelessness.
$750 million for the Portfolio Reinvestment Program, which provides funding to rehabilitate and extend the long-term affordability of state-funded rental multifamily housing projects that are at risk of conversion to market-rate housing.
$500 million for the Infill Infrastructure Grant Program . This would provide incentive grants to assist with new construction and rehabilitation of infrastructure that supports high-density affordable and mixed-income housing in locations designated as infill.
$450 million for the Joe Serna, Jr. Farmworker Housing Program to fund grants or loans for the construction or rehabilitation of housing for agricultural employees and their families.
$350 million for affordable student housing projects to be split evenly between the University of California and the California State University.
$200 million for a new Community Anti-Displacement and Preservation Program, which helps protect unsubsidized housing that may naturally be affordable and requires long-term affordability regulations.
$200 million for the Tribal Housing Grant Program which finances housing and housing-related activities to enable tribes to rebuild and reconstitute their communities.
$200 million to the Affordable Housing Innovation Fund for the Local Housing Trust Fund Matching Grant Program. This would fund competitive grants or loans to local housing trust funds that develop, own, lend, or invest in affordable housing and would be used to create pilot programs to demonstrate innovative approaches to creating or preserving affordable housing.
Homeownership
$1.25 billion for the CalVet Home Loan Program (https://www.calvet.ca.gov/HomeLoans) to help veterans and their families purchase homes. This portion of the bond would be repaid through mortgage (principal and interest) payments.
$600 million for the CalHome program. CalHome provides forgivable loans for lower-income households in self-help homeownership projects, including subdivisions and manufactured homes.
$500 million for the My Home downpayment assistance program to fund low-to-moderate income home purchase assistance programs.
What Benefits Would Prop. 1 Create for California’s Economy & Communities?
Prop. 1 would help expand and preserve California’s affordable housing supply while generating economic benefits and advancing the state’s housing goals. The bond would help close the financing gap for affordable rental homes, which serve lower-income California families and include seniors, people with disabilities, farmworkers, college students, and unhoused youth. According to legislative analyses (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billTextClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260SB417), the bond is expected to:
Produce more than 40,000 new affordable homes for lower-income families and individuals.
Preserve more than 5,500 existing affordable homes , ensuring they remain affordable for future generations.
Create more than 53,000 construction jobs through building new housing across the state.
Generate $1.3 billion in state and local tax revenue that supports local communities and public services.
Every $1 invested in state affordable housing leverages roughly $4 (https://roadmaphome.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/01/Roadmap-Home-Report-2026.pdf) in federal, local, and private investment, maximizing the impact of public dollars. Affordable housing also delivers economic, health, and environmental benefits (https://affordablehomes.calhousingpartnership.org/). For example:
Children who grow up in affordable housing earn a median of $51,000 more over their lifetimes,
Permanent supportive housing saves an estimated $1.80 in public costs for every $1 invested (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8863642/pdf/nihms-1768403.pdf), and
Building homes near jobs and transit lowers transportation costs while reducing greenhouse gas emissions (https://www.hcd.ca.gov/policy-and-research/intersectional-policy-work/housing-and-climate-change).
Together, these investments would expand housing opportunities, reduce housing instability, strengthen local economies, and help California meet its long-term housing needs.
How Would Prop. 1 Be Repaid?
Prop. 1 asks voters to authorize a total of $11.25 billion in GO bonds, divided as follows:
A $10 billion GO bond for affordable housing and homeownership programs that would be repaid from the state’s General Fund, and
A $1.25 billion veterans’ bond, a type of tax-exempt GO bond, for the CalVet Home Loan program that would be repaid through mortgage payments, with the General Fund as a backstop.
California voters often pass GO bonds to fund infrastructure projects that are designed to serve the public over many generations, as has been the case with affordable housing. Voters have also historically passed veterans’ bonds for CalVet to support homeownership opportunities for veterans.
GO bonds are repaid from the state’s General Fund. Repaying the $10 billion bond would cost $580 million per year for the next 30 years, for a total estimated cost of $17.4 billion ($10 billion in principal and $7.39 billion in interest). As of the governor’s proposed 2026-27 budget, California had $6.3 billion in General Fund debt service for GO bonds, or roughly 2.6% of General Fund expenditures.
In contrast, veterans bonds are generally self-supporting because they are repaid through principal and interest payments made by CalVet Home Loan Program borrowers. However, they are still GO bonds and are ultimately backed by the state’s General Fund. If program revenues were insufficient to cover the debt service, the General Fund would be responsible for the difference. It is unclear how often, if ever, the General Fund has had to backfill debt payments for previous veterans bonds.
Prop. 1 bond dollars would replenish depleted affordable housing programs. But bond dollars alone will not solve the housing shortage, nor would they replace the need for ongoing investments to meet the state’s substantial housing needs.
Prop. 1 and Prop. 38 Draw From Same Bonding Capacity, Face Important Trade Offs
Voters face two GO bond measures on the November 2026 ballot: Prop. 1 and Proposition 38. Prop. 38 would authorize $8.4 billion in GO bonds to support research and development in immunology and immunotherapy. Voters should weigh how each proposal addresses the state’s most pressing needs, fits within California’s limited borrowing capacity, and affects the state’s ability to invest in services that help families today and in the future.
Like all GO bonds, Prop. 38 would require long-term General Fund debt-service payments — estimated at $500 million annually (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Initiative/2025-026) for 25 years — reducing budget and bonding capacity for other state priorities. If both Prop. 1 and Prop. 38 are approved, it would reduce General Fund dollars by roughly $1.1 billion annually.
Public sector investment in scientific research is needed, particularly given federal cuts, but Prop. 38 raises important fiscal and policy considerations. GO bonds are conventionally used to finance infrastructure projects — like roads, bridges, or housing — that can be used over decades, roughly matching the time it takes to repay the bond itself.
Funding research through GO bonds does not work the same way. Bond-funded research gets most of the dollars upfront for grants, salaries, and operating costs, but are not guaranteed to be built into a lasting asset. Research findings do compound overtime, but the bond dollars themselves are depleted after a few years. The state then spends years or decades paying interest on bonds that stopped directly funding work long ago. So while scientific research needs funding, a GO bond is not the appropriate funding mechanism. Plus, half of Prop. 38’s funding would be concentrated on a limited set of health conditions, even though California already has multiple public and private research institutions (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Initiative/2025-026) conducting work in these areas.
Prop. 1 doesn’t confront these same challenges. While previous affordable housing bond dollars were also used up quickly, they left behind affordable homes that will continue to serve numerous families for decades. Affordable housing developments that use state dollars must have affordability requirements for at least 55 years — way beyond the repayment of the bonds with which they’re financed. The community benefits and capital assets outlast the debt, which is the intended purpose of GO bonds.
Prop. 1 Supporters and Opponents
Prop. 1 is supported by a broad coalition (https://www.housingbondca.com/coalition) of organizations representing housing, business, labor, local government, older adults, tenants, homelessness, urban planning, construction, environmental, and civil rights interests, among others.
Official opposition has been limited. The primary opponents on record include a few Republican state legislators who voted against (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billVotesClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260SB417) placing the measure on the ballot.

- Cost: $500-600M/year for ~25 years = ~0.25% of General Fund; total ~$17.4B principal+interest (~15% more in real terms than cash)

- Context: 2018 bond ($4B) exhausted by 2023; ~40,000 shovel-ready affordable units stalled for want of ~$4.1B more subsidy; Multifamily Housing Program oversubscribed 9:1; state allocated only ~$1.8B for affordable development in 2026 with no new ongoing funding
- 55-year affordability covenants > 25-30 year repayment: asset outlasts debt, textbook appropriate use of GO bonds
- Debt-service ratio currently ~3% of GF revenues, below historical ~4% average; adding Prop 1 + Prop 38 → ~3.5-3.8%
- No organized opposition campaign; $0 reported to No committee
- Polls: 55% Yes (Sept) → 60% Yes (Oct); forecast ~98.6% chance to pass

Arguments against:
- Structural deficits: LAO projects ~$18B problem in 2026-27, growing to ~$35B annually from 2027-28; debt service is legally fixed and crowds out discretionary spending in lean years
- State already carries ~$80B outstanding GF-supported debt + ~$40B authorized unsold; ~$6B/yr debt service
- Doesn't address root causes (cost of construction, permitting, land use)
- Pork-barrel spread: veterans only 11% of the total (and they repay it themselves) — name is arguably misleading
- Down payment assistance ($500M My Home, $600M CalHome) may bid up prices given supply constraints
- Editorial opposition: Bay Area News Group (Mercury News/East Bay Times), Sacramento Bee ran it, SD Union-Tribune, Daily Breeze/Daily News/Whittier, Press Democrat, LA Times columnist George Skelton, Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association
- Editorial support: SF Chronicle, McClatchy opinion board (yes), LWV California (yes), SPUR (yes), CalBudget Center analysis leans favorable

Weighing: The core question is whether $500-600M/year (0.25% of the General Fund) is worth unlocking ~40,000 permanently affordable homes (plus preservation and homeownership) that are already designed, entitled and partially financed, at ~$4 leverage per state dollar, financed against an asset with a 55-year affordability covenant.

Consider: 40,000 units × 55 years of affordability. Even at $250K state subsidy/unit, that's a very low cost per year of affordability delivered. Meanwhile, California spends far more on the downstream costs of homelessness (LAO/healthcare/criminal justice). Permanent supportive housing saves ~$1.80 per $1 invested in public costs.

The fiscal objections are real but modest in scale: 0.25% of the GF, and the DSR remains below its historical average even with Prop 1 and 38. The structural deficit argument proves too much — by that logic California could never make any capital investment, and the deficit is driven by health care, education, and pension costs, not by $580M in housing debt service. Also, capital assets with multi-decade useful lives are precisely what GO bonds are for; paying cash would be intergenerationally unfair.

The "doesn't fix root causes" critique is also weak as a reason to vote no: the Legislature has passed substantial streamlining (CEQA reform, builder's remedy, SB 407-era laws), and Prop 45 on the same ballot addresses permitting. The down-payment-assistance critique is the strongest substantive policy concern (could inflate prices), but it's only ~$1.1B of $10B, and it's targeted at low/moderate income with affordability restrictions.

The "veterans bait-and-switch" critique is a messaging complaint, not a policy defect — and the CalVet portion costs taxpayers nothing.

Given: no organized opposition, ~$0 in No funding, huge leverage, tiny relative fiscal cost, asset life far exceeding debt life, below-average debt ratio, and a documented ~40,000-unit shovel-ready backlog that needs roughly $4.1B... the balance clearly favors Yes.

## **YES**

**Prop 1 (Nov 3, 2026) — $11.25B housing bond. Vote YES.**

Why, based on the research:

**The value is unusually good.** The LAO projects up to **40,000 affordable rental units**, ~2,500 farmworker units, 1,200 student beds, plus preservation of 5,500+ existing affordable homes and homeownership help for up to 40,000 households — for roughly **$250K of state subsidy per unit**. Enterprise Community Partners found ~$3.60–$4 of federal/local/private money leveraged per state dollar.

**The money targets a documented, shovel-ready backlog.** ~39,880 units across 461 developments are fully designed, entitled and partially financed, stalled purely on a funding gap of about **$4.1B**. The 2018 bond was exhausted by 2023; the Multifamily Housing Program is oversubscribed ~9-to-1; the state allocated only ~$1.8B this year with no ongoing funding. This is the highest-leverage marginal dollar available, not speculative spending.

**The fiscal cost is small and the debt structure is appropriate.** $500–600M/year for ~25 years is **0.25% of the General Fund**. California's debt-service ratio is ~3% of GF revenues, *below* its ~4% historical average — even with Prop 1 and Prop 38 added. Critically, funded projects carry **55-year affordability covenants**, so the asset's useful life far exceeds the 25–30 year repayment. That is exactly what general obligation bonds are for; paying cash would shift the cost onto the low-income Californians who benefit decades out.

**The opposition is thin.** No argument against was submitted, **zero dollars** reported to any "No" committee, and the state Republican Party is officially *neutral*. Opposition is limited to a handful of legislators and some editorial boards.

**The best counterargument, and why it doesn't flip the vote:** LAO projects an ~$18B problem in 2026-27 growing to ~$35B annually, and debt service is legally fixed while program spending can be cut — so this does reduce flexibility (Skelton, Mercury News, U-T, Press Democrat, Howard Jarvis all make this case). But $580M isn't what's driving a structural deficit rooted in health care, education and pensions; by that logic California could never finance *any* long-lived capital asset. The "doesn't fix root causes" critique is also weak — the Legislature has already passed major streamlining (and Prop 45 addresses permitting on this same ballot). Funding and reform are complements. The genuine weaknesses — the somewhat misleading "Veterans" branding (11% of funds, and vets repay that part themselves) and ~$1.1B in down-payment assistance that could bid up prices — are real but small relative to the whole.

Bottom line: modest, below-historical-average debt cost against 40,000 permanently affordable homes that are already permitted and waiting. **Yes.**
